name: fastmod
baseline: Clang-generated code for 32-bit x % d and x / d with a compile-time-known divisor, and the hardware 32-bit division instruction
workload: Hashing-style benchmark on Intel Skylake built with Clang: run time in seconds versus divisor (3 to 63) for the hardware division instruction, compiler-generated code and the library's LKK approach (plot docs/hashbenches-skylake-clang.png shown in the README).
claimed_speedup: README text: 'In hashing benchmarks on Intel Skylake with Clang, this library outperforms compiler optimizations' and 'Faster than compiler-optimized divisions for known divisors'. Plot values read off the image (approximate, not printed as text): division instruction about 0.86 s for every divisor; compiler about 0.25-0.44 s; fastmod ('our approach (LKK)') about 0.25-0.30 s for most divisors and about 0.02 s at the power-of-two divisors 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. That is about 3x faster than the division instruction and up to about 1.7x faster than the compiler at the compiler's worst divisors (derived from plot reading); at some divisors (for example 3, 5, 6) the compiler line is level with or slightly below fastmod.
compiler_and_flags: Clang, version and flags not stated (README)
hardware: Intel Skylake, exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only (include/fastmod.h), C and C++. 32-bit operands on 64-bit hardware (64-bit variants are marked experimental). The multiplier M must be precomputed once per divisor (computeM_u32), so the win needs a divisor reused across many operations. fastdiv requires d > 1; signed fastdiv must avoid d in {-1, 1, INT32_MIN}.
caveats: The only quantitative evidence in the README is a plot image with no numbers in the text; values above were read off the image by eye. Clang version, flags and exact CPU are missing and the hashing workload behind the plot is not described or linked (the repo has tests/modnbenchmark.cpp and tests/moddivnbenchmark.cpp for 64-bit operations, whose results are not published). Chart is first-party. Peer-reviewed paper (Lemire, Kaser, Kurz, Software: Practice and Experience 2019, arXiv 1902.01961) could not be opened here (arxiv.org, ar5iv, r-libre.teluq.ca, gmplib.org and emergentmind.com blocked); a search-result snippet only said the paper's C implementations beat state-of-the-art compilers on Skylake and Ryzen 'sometimes by more than 25%' and reported 18 cycles (LKK) versus 72 cycles (division instruction) on Skylake with GCC and Clang. That is snippet-only and not verified, but suggests a paper-access retier to B or A. Category set to big-integer-arbitrary-precision as the closest wave-8 category; the guessed blas-lapack is wrong (integer division, not linear algebra).

name: fCWT
baseline: PyWavelets (pywt.cwt), MATLAB cwt, SciPy, ssqueezepy, CCWT, Rwave (C), Wavelib (C++) and Mathematica CWT implementations
workload: Continuous wavelet transform of synthetic signals, 10k or 100k samples with 300 or 3000 frequencies; README says fCWT C++ is run with 8 threads and exhaustive FFTW plans (its own benchmark target).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Calculating CWT 34-120x faster than all competitors' (C++ performance). Table (seconds, 10k-300 / 10k-3000 / 100k-300 / 100k-3000): fCWT C++ 0.005 / 0.04 / 0.03 / 0.32; PyWavelets 0.10 / 1.17 / 1.06 / 12.69; Matlab 0.75 / 0.86 / 1.06 / 13.26; ssqueezepy 0.04 / 0.43 / 1.16 / 17.76; SciPy 0.19 / 1.82 / 2.11 / 18.70; Rwave (C) 0.18 / 1.84 / 2.28 / 23.22; Mathematica - / - / - / 27.83; Wavelib (C++) 0.25 / 2.55 / 4.85 / 45.04; CCWT (Python) 0.019 / 0.11 / 0.15 / 3.40. README 'speedup factor' column: PyWavelets 34.29x, Matlab 35.85x, SciPy 50.54x, Rwave 62.75x, Wavelib 121.72x, CCWT 10.63x. fCWT Python wrapper 0.66 s and Matlab wrapper 1.55 s at 100k-3000.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated. CMakeLists.txt sets '-fPIC -mavx -O2' on Unix ('/arch:AVX /O2' on MSVC), default build type Release, OpenMP; README says FFTW must be built with OpenMP and AVX to reproduce the table.
hardware: MacBook Pro 2019, 2.3 GHz Intel Core i9 (4.5 GHz boost), 16 GB 2400 MHz DDR4
stars_or_usage: 402 stars; cited in a Nature Computational Science 2022 paper
tradeoffs: Single-precision (float) CWT with Morlet wavelet; built on FFTW with OpenMP and AVX. The repo's libs/ directory ships prebuilt FFTW3 binaries (fftw3f, OpenMP) and omp.h; FFTW is GPL-2.0-or-later, so the fCWT source is Apache-2.0 but a build linking those binaries is GPL. Python (pip fcwt) and MATLAB MEX wrappers are slower than the C++ build (README says Matlab path loses performance).
caveats: Evidence is the README table, which the README says reproduces the Nature Computational Science paper (Arts and van den Broek, 2022, cover article); the paper itself could not be opened (nature.com and doi.org blocked), so B rests on the README's statement. Benchmark code is public (src/benchmark.cpp, fCWT_benchmark; Wavelib and Rwave rows run by it, Python/Matlab/Mathematica scripts under src/benchmark per the README) and hardware is stated, but the compiler is not, so it falls short of A. fCWT is run with 8 threads and exhaustive FFTW plans; thread counts of the competitors are not stated. The README's own factors do not match its table ratios (for example PyWavelets 12.69 s / fCWT 0.32 s is about 39.7x, listed 34.29x; Wavelib 45.04 / 0.32 is about 141x, listed 121.72x), and the Matlab row (0.75 s at 10k-300 versus 0.86 s at 10k-3000) looks odd. The baselines are other CWT libraries; fCWT itself uses FFTW, so the guessed FFTW baseline does not apply. Python and Matlab rows compare through wrappers.

name: FFTW
baseline: FFTPACK (netlib FFTPACK v4, C translation as built in the PFFFT benchmark)
workload: Single-precision complex and real FFTs of power-of-two sizes 2^1 to 2^21, measured in MFLOPS (5 N log2 N for complex, 2.5 N log2 N for real) with the PFFFT benchmark harness; columns FFTW F(estim) (FFTW_ESTIMATE) and FFTW F(auto) (planner-chosen) against FFTPack.
claimed_speedup: Complex single precision, MFLOPS, FFTPack versus FFTW F(estim) / F(auto): N=64 7543 vs 34957 / 40030 (about 4.6x / 5.3x, derived from page data); N=1024 8579 vs 49570 / 55947 (about 5.8x / 6.5x, derived); N=2^16 7382 vs 20507 (about 2.8x, F(estim), derived). Real single precision: N=64 6193 vs 7555 / 11762; N=1024 8593 vs 18015 / 25766 (about 2.1x / 3.0x, derived). Reversal at the largest complex sizes: N=2^20 FFTPack 5312 vs FFTW F(estim) 4915, N=2^21 4952 vs 2511 (FFTW slower).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3.0 (from the result file name). Harness defaults in marton78/pffft bench/CMakeLists.txt are Release, -march=native (BENCH_ARCH) and fast math ON for the code it builds; FFTW is linked as a system-installed libfftw3 (the PFFFT README names the Debian/Ubuntu package libfftw3-dev), so its version and build flags are not recorded.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U, Ubuntu 20.04.1 LTS x64 (from the result file name)
stars_or_usage: 3.1k stars; PFFFT README says 99% of open-source projects needing an FFT use FFTW
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0-or-later (copyleft). The GitHub repo holds only the codelet generator, not generated C source: build from the official tarballs at fftw.org. Planning cost (estimate versus measure/patient/exhaustive) is not included in the MFLOPS figures. Not header-only; large API surface (multi-dimensional, r2r, MPI, threads).
caveats: Third-party harness written by the author of the rival PFFFT library, but the result favours FFTW, so no sign of bias; the result file does not state FFTW's version or flags, and the benchmark was run on a 2017-era laptop CPU, so tier B rather than A (flags only inferable from the harness defaults). The FFTW F(auto) column is 0.000000 for N >= 4096 (not measured). FFTPACK is 1985 scalar code and the FFTW rows use SIMD, so the gap partly reflects SIMD rather than algorithm; FFTW F(estim) is slower than FFTPACK for complex N >= 2^20 on this machine. FFTW's own benchFFT results (fftw.org/speed, Frigo and Johnson, Proc. IEEE 2005) are the original evidence but fftw.org and the paper could not be opened here (EGRESS_BLOCKED). The PFFFT README (marton78/pffft) also states FFTPACK 'is not competitive with the fastest ones, such as FFTW, Intel MKL, AMD ACML, Apple vDSP'. Homepage http://www.fftw.org/ was not reachable, so repo_url is the GitHub mirror.

name: FLINT
baseline: GMP (Chudnovsky pi program and naive mpz_t addmul matrix multiplication), MPFR (mpfr_const_pi), Pari/GP (t_MAT multiplication)
workload: Computing pi to 100 million digits, and multiplying two 100 x 100 integer matrices with b-bit entries (b = 10, 100, 1000), FLINT fmpz_t/fmpz_mat_mul versus GMP mpz_t and Pari/GP.
claimed_speedup: Page text: FLINT's own integer and floating-point code 'can be 2-10 times faster in many typical applications'. Pi to 100M digits: GMP-chudnovsky 62.1 s, MPFR mpfr_const_pi 172.9 s, FLINT arb_const_pi 31.6 s (about 2x GMP, 5x MPFR) and 9.34 s on 8 threads. 100x100 integer matrix multiply, seconds for b = 10 / 100 / 1000: GMP mpz_t naive 0.0122 / 0.0172 / 0.159; Pari/GP optimized 0.00147 / 0.00920 / 0.102; FLINT fmpz_mat_mul 0.0000678 / 0.00235 / 0.0456 (8 threads 0.0000675 / 0.000800 / 0.0142); FLINT naive fmpz_addmul 0.00395 / 0.0213 / 0.163 (about 3x faster than GMP at b = 10, about 20% slower at b = 100, per page text).
hardware: 8-core AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U (Zen 3); FLINT configured with the BLAS backend for modular matrix multiplication
stars_or_usage: 662 stars; used by SageMath, msolve, FIRE and CM per the applications page; python-flint bindings
tradeoffs: Built on GMP/MPFR (or compatible); FLINT 3 absorbed Arb, Antic and Calcium; the optimized matmul is multimodular and wins over a naive big-integer loop mostly for algorithmic reasons. fft_small (needs AVX2 or NEON) is the newer small-prime FFT for large integer and polynomial products. LGPL-3.0-or-later.
caveats: Numbers come from the project's own website, read here from its page source in github.com/flintlib/flintwebpage (src/applications.txt) because flintlib.org, fredrikj.net and the benchmarks page are blocked here. First-party; compiler and flags not stated, no benchmark code linked, so tier C. The matrix comparison pits FLINT's optimized multimodular algorithm against naive GMP loops (not like-for-like kernels); FLINT's naive fmpz_addmul is slower than GMP at b = 100 and b = 1000 (0.0213 vs 0.0172, 0.163 vs 0.159). The y-cruncher row on the same page (18.3 s single core) is faster than FLINT's pi. This repo already has FLINT records from wave 8 (w8-bigint-gh-cpp, w8-bigint-papers) with the same evidence at flintlib.org/applications.html; this record cites the page's source file instead. The guessed category fft is wrong, FLINT is number theory and bigint arithmetic.
